newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kabila's U.N. envoy to improve new Congo's image.
newsitem.headline: Kabila's U.N. envoy to improve new Congo's image.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's newly appointed ambassador to the United Nations said he would seek to improve the image of the former Zaire abroad after years of neglect.
In an interview with Reuters, Andre Kapanga reiterated the desire of what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo for an investigation into alleged massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees.
"We would like to improve the image of the country. If you look back at the last seven years, you will see that Zaire was neglected by the Zairean government," Kapanga said.

"Now we have Congo, we would like to show that the leaders of this country care about their country, and they would like to show to the world that they are here to work for the people rather than for themselves," he added.
Kabila grabbed power in May after a seven-month bush war which swept away veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko.
Kabila's Tutsi-dominated forces have been accused of slaughtering thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees in the east of the former Zaire. Kabila has rejected the accusations.
About 1.5 million Rwandan Hutus, including soldiers of the former FAR national army, streamed into Zaire during the civil war in Rwanda in 1994.
Up to 700,000 returned home in the early stage of Kabila's rebellion last year when their refugee camps were overrun by the Zairean rebels.
Of the remainder, some have died from exhaustion and hunger, as they fled the fast-moving frontline inside the former Zaire.
But at least 150,000 refugees are still unaccounted for by U.N officials.
The U.N. secretary-general has named Atsu-Koffi Amega, a former judge of the Togolese Supreme Court, as head of a team to conduct a probe into the alleged killings.

Kabila's government persuaded the U.N. to change the head of the investigation after it accused the man first appointed, Chilean human rights lawyer Roberto Garreton, of bias. Garreton has published reports accusing Kabila's forces and their allies of massacres.
"We welcome (the new) appointment. We want them to come and carry out their mission. We don't want them to drag this thing for a long time," Kapanga said.
He said the soldiers of Kabila's Alliance committed no massacres during their whirlwind campaign against Mobutu and hoped that the whole truth would come out after the U.N. probe.

"We strongly believe we did not commit any massacre. We strongly believe that if the investigation is carried out appropriately, you will see that many of the deaths occured as a result of the war that was taking place, as a result of malnutrition and diseases," he said.
Kapanga's predecessor at the U.N., Lubaji Khabouji, died earlier this month.
